title: Legacy-client compatibility blocks shared runtime upgrades
pattern: A shared mainline or high-level business path retains obsolete target, runtime, or compiler workarounds (pointer-width checks, archaic target flags, compiler-version fallbacks) solely for a small set of legacy clients who refuse to upgrade, preventing normal upgrades for every other consumer.
why_bad: A small legacy population imposes target-specific complexity on unrelated systems and holds the entire transitive closure of dependencies hostage, delaying security patches, performance optimizations, standard compiler upgrades, and modern language features across the ecosystem.
detection:
The linter must observe:
1. Platform/compiler-specific checks or configurations (`cfg` flags, pointer-width or archaic target OS checks, compiler-version fallbacks) embedded in shared libraries or high-level business logic.
2. The check exists exclusively to maintain compatibility with a specific, obsolete client environment and holds back the shared dependency/toolchain upgrade.
Do not infer obsolescence or customer refusal merely from a `cfg` flag or a 32-bit target; legitimate supported targets are exempt.
counterexample:
`Context-dependent`
Legitimate current multi-platform/hardware-abstraction support; legacy workloads already isolated from the shared mainline in their own runtime or containerized deployment.
```rust
// Valid: Legitimate multi-platform support in a hardware-abstracting library
```
source: - Titus Winters et al., *Software Engineering at Google* (2020) [348]; *Software Engineering at Google (Winters et al.), Chapter 21, p. 454 [194, 1045]*
